segments.text: American Fork City Council — Regular Session — August 25, 2026:

Aaron Booker, a nonresident, criticized what he viewed as inconsistent enforcement of meeting decorum and a broader pattern of selective enforcement within the City and Police Department. He urged City officials to apply standards equally, protect First Amendment rights, and pursue meaningful reform.

Daniel Sroka urged the City to take action to restore public trust in the Police Department, suggesting policy revisions, improved body cameras, or a resident review board. Citing public critiques of body-camera footage, Mr. Sroka called for meaningful reform and emphasized the importance of protecting constitutional rights.

Debbie Shaw described her family’s longstanding service to American Fork and raised concerns about alleged civil-rights violations involving her son and others. She requested a fair, transparent, and independent review of the Police Department and urged City leadership to restore public trust through accountability and action.

Jan Chamberlain, a member of the NO ICE in Utah County Coalition, requested a meeting with City officials to discuss immigration enforcement policies. She supported lawful due process while encouraging a humanitarian approach that protects innocent immigrants and children. She also asked the City to consider policies limiting the use of municipal property and local law-enforcement resources for federal immigration enforcement.

Mary Mitchell an American Fork resident supported an independent review of the Police Department and urged the city to rebuild public trust, particularly among vulnerable and immigrant communities. She requested greater transparency regarding the Police Department’s cooperation with ICE under Utah County’s 287(g) Agreement, citing concerns about racial profiling and residents becoming afraid to contact law enforcement.

Roy Shaw, an American Fork resident, requested an independent third-party review of the Police Department’s accountability, leadership, and handling of alleged misconduct. He stated that the review should determine whether systemic or leadership failures exist, restore public confidence, and guide any appropriate personnel action. He also expressed concern that similar requests from residents had received no meaningful response.
Andrea Tamita, a 93-year-old American Fork citizen, urged City officials and residents to address wrongdoing, hold public officials and safety patrols accountable, and protect children.

Elizabeth Oscarson, an American Fork resident, opposed ICE activity within the city and stated that residents deserve to feel safe. She requested complete transparency and public reporting regarding interactions between City departments and federal immigration authorities.

Gregory Titus stated that his and his wife’s constitutional rights had been violated in American Fork. He expressed a willingness to work with City officials and invited them to contact him regarding his concerns.

entities.speaker: Anna Montoya
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Ms. Montoya summarized that the City Council adopted the fiscal year 2026–2027 interim budget on June 23. The budget included a proposed $660,000 property-tax increase to partially staff a new fire station. The original proposal would cost the average homeowner approximately $33 annually, or $2.78 per month, representing an increase of about 8.5%. Because the increase required a truth-in-taxation process, the city held a public hearing on August 11.

Ms. Montoya reported that, after adopting the interim budget, the City realized approximately $100,000 in insurance-premium savings. Those savings would allow the Council to reduce the proposed tax increase while maintaining the planned fire-station staffing. The revised increase would cost the average homeowner approximately $2.40 per month and represent an annual increase of about 7.4%. She noted that the Council could reduce the proposed tax increase further, including in response to concerns raised about economic-development spending. However, any additional reduction would require corresponding amendments to other budget line items to preserve full funding for the planned fire-station staffing. She directed the Council to the suggested motions and emphasized that members could propose additional budget changes.

Ms. Montoya clarified that the proposed $120,000 playground deferral would delay a capital project and would not require the use of reserves. However, because it represents one-time savings, it would not permanently fund the City’s ongoing operating expenses, leaving the budget gap to be addressed the following year. She explained that five vehicle leases were also expiring during the current year. Staff did not recommend extending the leases, so purchasing vehicles would require up to approximately $345,000 from reserves. This expenditure likewise would not resolve the structural operating deficit. She added that the city has approximately two dozen leased vehicles requiring replacement over the next several years, meaning similar funding decisions would arise again in future budgets.

entities.speaker: Clark P. Taylor
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Council Member Taylor stated that he remained reluctant to support a property-tax increase but recognized that rising costs make it difficult for the City to continue providing essential services, particularly public safety, without additional revenue. He suggested that the city explore changes to its budgeting practices in the future to help address increasing costs. He recalled that, during the City’s 2021 Truth-in-Taxation process, the first since 2008—residents expressed a preference for smaller, more frequent adjustments rather than substantial increases after long intervals. He opposed using the City’s reserves to cover ongoing expenses and indicated that he favored reducing the proposed increase from 8.7% to 5.7%. He noted that the revised increase would cost the average resident less than $2 per month and stated that, although he was not comfortable with any increase, he intended to support the reduced proposal.

Council Member Taylor explained that the proposal to use reserves likely originated from a suggestion he made after previously stating that he would not support a tax increase. He had asked whether the city could use reserves on a one-time basis to proceed with the fire station and then adjust future budgets to accommodate its ongoing costs. He clarified that it was a preliminary idea that he had raised without fully analyzing its long-term implications.

entities.speaker: Ernie John
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Council Member John agreed with Council Member Taylor and opposed using reserves to fund ongoing operations. He noted that the City’s strong bond rating helps it secure favorable financing terms and potentially save residents millions of dollars. He cautioned that continued use of reserves could jeopardize that rating and create significant long- term costs.

Council Member John supported the reduced tax-increase proposal identified as Operational Amendment B. He commended staff for identifying savings and emphasized the importance of retaining some economic-development funding because those efforts can generate sales-tax revenue and strengthen the City’s overall tax base.

Council Member John emphasized that supporting the increase was not an easy decision and expressed appreciation to staff for identifying a reduced option. He noted that he was approaching retirement and had spoken with many residents living on fixed incomes. He said those residents overwhelmingly preferred smaller, more manageable increases rather than waiting several years and then facing a substantial adjustment.

Although some residents had opposed any increase, Council Member John stated that more of the people who contacted him favored avoiding large, infrequent increases. He acknowledged that inflation was also increasing the City’s operating costs and concluded that he did not see another practical way to maintain necessary services.

entities.speaker: Ryan Hunter
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Council Member Hunter agreed that the proposed increase was consistent with residents’ comments during the 2021 Truth-in-Taxation process favoring smaller, incremental adjustments instead of infrequent, substantial increases. He noted that the current proposal was limited partly because the city had identified other funding and used reserves to cover certain costs. He supported developing a formal strategy for replenishing reserves after they are used, comparing reserves to a household savings account from which money may be withdrawn for an unexpected expense and then repaid. He suggested that future budgets include a repayment schedule, potentially spanning two or three years, so the City could restore funds used for major capital needs such as wells or fire-station construction.

Council Member Hunter opposed using capital reserves for recurring expenditures or routine vehicle purchases but acknowledged that reserves can appropriately cover significant upfront capital costs. He suggested that modest annual adjustments, possibly tied to a defined rate or repayment metric, could help rebuild those reserves. However, he cautioned against treating annual tax increases as automatic or expected and emphasized that any incremental adjustment should be connected to a clear plan for repaying the City’s reserves.

Council Member Hunter explained that he raised the issue of incremental increases because residents had specifically requested that approach during the 2021 Truth-in- Taxation process. He observed that, had the Council implemented increases of even 1.5% annually since then, the cumulative increase would have remained below 6%, and the city might not have needed an increase that year. He disagreed that residents would benefit from retaining and investing the money between less-frequent tax increases. He noted that residents living paycheck to paycheck generally do not have discretionary income available to invest and may find small, predictable annual adjustments easier to absorb than a larger increase imposed at one time.

Council Member Hunter acknowledged that routine annual increases could cause the Council to become complacent about the burden placed on residents. He emphasized that each adjustment should still receive careful scrutiny and consideration of the sacrifices required from taxpayers. Nevertheless, he believed the preference for smaller incremental increases had been clearly expressed in 2021, particularly by residents experiencing financial hardship who lacked the means to invest any temporary savings.

entities.speaker: Staci Carroll
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Council Member Carroll acknowledged that increasing taxes is difficult even when the need is clear, emphasizing that the Council understands the financial burden on residents and takes such decisions seriously. She explained that staffing the new fire station was a high priority because firefighter salaries are an ongoing operating expense that must be permanently incorporated into the City’s budget rather than funded as a one-time capital cost.

Council Member Carroll commended staff for finding a way to cover approximately $1.6 million in staffing costs while initially requesting only $660,000 in additional property tax revenue and then identifying an option to reduce the increase further. She stated that providing 24-hour public-safety coverage to that area of the city justified the additional cost, as reduced or intermittent coverage would be inadequate. Although reluctant to raise taxes, Council Member Carroll indicated that she would support the reduced 5.7% increase.

entities.speaker: Tim Holley
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text:
Council Member Holley asked for clarification regarding Option C. He recalled that the earlier discussion focused on delaying certain capital projects, including playground improvements and lease-purchase expenditures, rather than using reserves. He questioned whether Option C had subsequently changed to include reserve funding and acknowledged that he may have missed updated information because he had been unable to meet with staff as planned.

Council Member Holley reiterated that he would vote against a property-tax increase because residents were already facing substantial increases in their household expenses. He stated that he had proposed several alternatives, although he acknowledged that not all were ideal, and expressed concern that none had been implemented. He also remained dissatisfied with how the purpose and proposed use of the tax increase had been communicated.

Council Member Holley suggested that, if additional funding or reserves were needed, the city could reconsider approximately $600,000 associated with a proposed reconfiguration of the fitness center’s weight area. He cited his own City utility bill, which had risen from approximately $110 to $130 per month in less than three years, as an example of the increasing financial burden on residents. He disagreed with the preference for smaller, more frequent tax increases. He argued that less-frequent increases could be financially preferable because residents could retain and potentially invest the money between adjustments. Although he respected the other Council members’ positions and acknowledged that his view might differ from theirs, he stated that he could not support the proposed increase in good conscience.

Council Member Holley responded that a household must have the additional money available to pay any tax increase, regardless of whether it is imposed incrementally or less frequently. He reasoned that, if residents can afford the additional tax, they could otherwise retain or invest that money; if they cannot afford it, they would be unable to pay the increased tax.

entities.speaker: Bradley J. Frost
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Mayor Frost stated that the budget process, which began in February, would conclude that evening. He emphasized that the budget is one of the Council’s most important responsibilities because it establishes priorities and funds services affecting residents. He thanked Ms. Montoya, Mr. Bunker, department heads, and staff, for the many hours devoted to preparing the budget and noted that work on the next budget would begin in approximately five months.
